reasoning_note: Outbound FTP from clinical subnet at 2:47 AM is highly suspicious; FTP is unencrypted and shouldn't be used for patient data.
Billing user accessing 47 records could be normal end-of-day reconciliation but the late hour warrants a check.
Admin VLAN connecting to medical device VLAN via SMB is a segmentation violation that could endanger device integrity.
Lab system sending 340 MB via SFTP to an external IP could be exfiltration of patient lab results and needs immediate containment.
Infusion pump reaching out to an external IP is a patient safety concern even if HTTPS; pumps should never talk to the internet.
High-volume DNS from a medical device could be DNS tunneling or just a misconfiguration, not sure which.
Nurse accessing 31 records across three departments at 2:30 AM is unusual; could be a float nurse but the volume and hour are concerning.
ICMP sweep from management VLAN could be legitimate IT scanning but I'm not aware of any scheduled scan today.
RDP from admin to the device VLAN on a Saturday morning is unusual and could allow unauthorized changes to medical devices.
Large PACS transfer could be a teleradiology send but 4.8 GB to an unknown external IP should be verified with radiology.
Another large PACS outbound transfer at 4 AM; could be scheduled replication but the external destination is unfamiliar to me.
Medical device communicating via unknown proprietary wireless to an unknown device is a serious patient safety and security risk.
Service account pulling 312 records across all departments in 8 minutes at 1 AM looks like automated data harvesting.
Ventilator using Telnet is a direct patient safety threat; Telnet is unencrypted and ventilators should have locked-down communications.
EHR to backup server via SMB during business hours looks like a scheduled backup job; 28 GB is large but destination is internal backup.
Pharmacy system sending 890 MB outbound on a Saturday at 3 AM is odd but could be a vendor update or reporting job I'm not aware of.
Patient monitor at 5x normal traffic at 3 AM is a clinical safety concern; could indicate device malfunction or compromise.
EHR server scanning all internal subnets on common attack ports at 3 AM is textbook lateral movement from a compromised critical system.
Physician accessing 22 records via VPN in the evening is consistent with normal after-hours charting or patient follow-up.
Nurse workstation exfiltrating 1.1 GB in 3 minutes to an external IP is almost certainly data theft or malware beaconing.

q21_note: Alerts identify device IPs and protocols but lack patient-facing context like which patients or units are affected, so clinical staff would need help interpreting the risk.
q22_note: The alerts provide enough technical detail including IPs, protocols, volumes, and timestamps to justify escalation and isolation actions to a security lead.
